whyCorrect: The sentence says painters put up with a slow, dangerous material because nothing else was so ____, so the blank has to name the one property that made the trouble worth it. The passage already named it: the carbonate "covered better than any other pigment then available." Covering power — hiding what is underneath — is opacity.

whyWrong.A: Transparent is the opposite of covering well; a transparent white would show the ground through it.
whyWrong.C: Portable is never at issue in the text, which describes a pigment made in buried pots and ground in the shop, not carried anywhere.
whyWrong.D: Colourful contradicts the description of the pigment as white, and colour is not the quality the passage praises.

tips: Find the sentence just before the blank that states the material's advantage — the blank is usually a one-word restatement of it.

whyCorrect: Everything the navigator does in the passage is mental bookkeeping: he watches stars rise and set, treats the canoe as stationary, and counts off the bearing of an island he cannot even see. No chart, log, or device is mentioned anywhere. The blank must say the reckoning is carried entirely in memory.

whyWrong.A: In company would mean the work is shared among several people, but the passage describes a single navigator's method, not a group effort.
whyWrong.B: On paper contradicts the passage — nothing is written down; the bearings are counted off mentally.
whyWrong.D: By instrument is exactly what the method avoids; the navigator's references are stars and an unseen island, not a compass or sextant.

whyCorrect: Read the sentence with each meaning substituted in. The surrounding text is about ball clay blended with coarse sand, and the underlined word names the thing "a workshop settles on" as a compromise between workability and kiln behaviour. That thing is the clay recipe itself — the prepared mixture the potter throws.

whyWrong.B: The everyday anatomical sense has nothing to do with a mixture of clay and sand; no person or animal appears in the text.
whyWrong.C: The sense meaning the main part of a document would need a written work in the context, and there is none.
whyWrong.D: The sense meaning an organized group of people cannot be "settled on" as a compromise between the wheel and the fire.

tips: For underlined-word questions, plug each option's meaning into the sentence literally — three of them will produce nonsense in that context.

whyCorrect: The passage is about printing economics: resetting type costs as much again, while pulling extra sheets from standing type costs almost nothing but paper. What a publisher must decide before the first sheet is pulled is therefore how many copies to print. That quantity is the print run.

whyWrong.A: The animal-enclosure sense is unrelated to type, paper, or presses.
whyWrong.B: A continuous period of a condition would make the sentence say a publisher fixes a stretch of time, which does not follow from a discussion of paper and press costs.
whyWrong.D: A regularly scheduled vehicle journey is a transport sense with no connection to a publisher's decision about printing.

whyCorrect: The passage contrasts plain lead, which casts "soft corners" and crumbling shoulders, with the tin-and-antimony alloy, which expands as it sets and so is forced into every angle of the mould. The result is a letter with crisp, well-defined edges. The blank names that quality of the face — its sharpness.

whyWrong.B: Colour of the metal is never discussed; the comparison is entirely about how well the letterform is reproduced.
whyWrong.C: Weight is closer to the property of "the bar it casts," which the sentence explicitly says is not the founder's reason.
whyWrong.D: Cheapness is contradicted by the passage, since the founder is adding tin and antimony to plain lead rather than economizing.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes hand papermaking, the underlined sentence describes the machine that replaced it, and the last sentence lists what followed — no deckle edges, arbitrary sheet sizes, lengths no longer limited by a man's reach. The underlined sentence is the hinge: it names the new method whose effects the closing sentence spells out.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text says printers kept preferring handmade paper; the text tracks what the machine changed, not resistance to it.
whyWrong.B: The thousand-sheets-a-day figure is in the first sentence, not the underlined one.
whyWrong.C: The text raises no doubt about who deserves credit; it simply names the patent.

tips: For function questions, check what the sentences on either side are doing — the underlined one usually connects them.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the drawback of fumigation, the underlined sentence introduces the nitrogen method, and the last sentence weighs that method's cost in time against its clean result. So the underlined sentence sets up the option the rest of the text evaluates.

whyWrong.A: The residues are described in the sentence before the underlined one, not in it.
whyWrong.C: The underlined sentence says the low-oxygen treatment kills the larvae; it concedes no failure. The only cost admitted anywhere is the three weeks it takes.
whyWrong.D: The text never addresses why beetles infest wood; it addresses how to get rid of them.

whyCorrect: The main idea has to cover the whole text, and the text does two things: it explains why raised fields resist frost (the ridge sits above the pooling cold air and the channels release stored heat overnight) and then reports that rebuilt plots survived frosts that killed neighbouring flat fields. Only one option carries both the mechanism and the evidence.

whyWrong.A: Reach of harvesters is never mentioned; the passage explains the platforms in terms of temperature, not convenience.
whyWrong.C: Irrigation in dry months is a plausible-sounding purpose but the text assigns the channels a thermal role — storing and releasing heat.
whyWrong.D: This reverses the evidence, which shows raised plots outperforming flat ones under frost.

whyCorrect: The text makes one claim and then qualifies it: tin makes the lead glaze opaque and white, so cheap red or buff earthenware comes out of the kiln looking like fine ware and the painter gets a white ground; but the raw glaze absorbs a brushstroke instantly, so nothing can be undone. The main idea has to include both the benefit and that single stated cost.

whyWrong.A: Firing temperature is never mentioned, let alone compared with porcelain's.
whyWrong.B: The text says the painter works with something like a porcelain decorator's freedom — it never claims painters preferred earthenware, and the buff or red colour is the problem the glaze hides, not an attraction.
whyWrong.C: This reverses the chemistry the text gives: the tin oxide is what makes the lead glaze opaque.

whyCorrect: Lindqvist's claim is specific: the diarist treats depot-laying, not the later journey, as the decisive work. The quotation therefore has to show the writer measuring the depot work by its consequences for the main party. Only one option does that — falling short of the depot site is described as a burden transferred to the spring party, when they can least bear it.

whyWrong.A: A lame pony is a hardship of the season but says nothing about the depots mattering more than the journey.
whyWrong.C: Reading aloud in the tent is camp routine and bears on neither depots nor the journey.
whyWrong.D: An admiring note about the evening light describes the scenery, not the importance of the depot work.

tips: Match the quotation to the exact comparison in the claim — here, depots weighed against the journey — not just to the general topic.

whyCorrect: The authority's point requires two facts held side by side: the quay with the largest tonnage was not the fastest at turning ships round. North Quay is the tonnage leader at 410 thousand tonnes yet takes 31 hours, while East Jetty moves nearly as much, 390 thousand tonnes, in only 19. Citing both is what shows tonnage alone to be a poor measure.

whyWrong.A: Old Basin's figures are accurate but it is neither the top-tonnage quay nor the fastest, so it cannot demonstrate the mismatch the authority describes.
whyWrong.B: Ferry Quay's 12 hours is the shortest time, but it also handles the least cargo, so this comparison never involves the busiest quay.
whyWrong.C: This gives only East Jetty's tonnage and omits any turnaround time, so no contrast between cargo and speed is made.

whyCorrect: Vandenberg claims the conservator put reversibility ahead of how the finished panel looked. The quotation needs to show her deliberately choosing the less effective option because it can be undone. Picking the weaker adhesive, in full knowledge that the stronger one holds better but cannot be removed without taking paint with it, is exactly that trade-off.

whyWrong.B: Counting the losses along an edge is a condition report, and involves no choice at all.
whyWrong.C: This is the opposite of the claim: it shows her giving extra time to the most visible passage, prioritizing appearance.
whyWrong.D: Photographing before treatment is standard documentation and shows nothing about what she added or whether it could be removed.

whyCorrect: Two facts control the ending. The alkaline reserve neutralises acid as it is produced, so it works on future damage, and the sentence itself states the treatment cannot restore strength already lost. Together those limit the treatment's value to preventing further deterioration.

whyWrong.A: Identifying the mill is a bibliographic question the passage never raises; deacidification tells you nothing about origin.
whyWrong.C: The sentence explicitly denies this — the treatment cannot give back lost strength.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the text concerns removing images or recycling fibre; the aim is to keep the sheet intact.

whyCorrect: The problem the passage sets out is uneven cooling: the surface sets first while the inside is still contracting, and the trapped strain can shatter the piece days later. The heated tunnel "lets the whole thickness come down together," so its purpose is to make the different parts cool at the same rate.

whyWrong.A: Shaping is finished at the blowing iron; the tunnel is a cooling stage, and nothing in the text describes it altering form.
whyWrong.C: The tunnel is heated only enough to slow the fall in temperature — the passage never suggests it exceeds furnace heat, and reheating that far would undo the piece.
whyWrong.D: Scratch resistance is a surface-hardness idea the text never raises; the danger described is internal strain.

whyCorrect: "Each female stocks a row of cells ... and seals them off with mud" and "a garden wall fitted with bundles of cut stems will hold hundreds of them by the second season" are both complete sentences. Two independent clauses can be joined with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, which is what the comma before and does here.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon already does the whole job of joining two independent clauses; adding and after it is redundant and non-standard.
whyWrong.B: A colon must follow a complete clause and introduce an explanation or list, not a second clause led by and.
whyWrong.C: With no comma, the reader first takes "mud and a garden wall" as a compound object of with and has to back up — the comma is what marks where the second clause starts.

commonMistakes: Choosing the semicolon because both halves are complete sentences, without noticing the and that comes after it.

whyCorrect: "The mechanism needs three things" is a complete sentence, and what follows is a list naming those three things. A colon after a complete clause is the standard way to introduce such a list.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation at all, the list runs straight into the clause and "three things a drop of water" reads as a single garbled phrase.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon must separate two independent clauses; the list of three items that follows is not a clause.
whyWrong.D: A comma plus and makes the drop of water look like a fourth item added to the sentence rather than the first of the three being introduced.

whyCorrect: Both halves stand alone: "The figure printed beside a shoal is therefore not the depth a ship will find there" and "it is the depth it can count on finding at almost any state of the tide." With no coordinating conjunction between them, a semicolon is the punctuation that joins two complete sentences.

whyWrong.A: A colon followed by and it is not a recognized way to link clauses; a colon introduces an explanation or list directly, without a conjunction.
whyWrong.C: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the two clauses run together, so the reader reads "find there it is" as one string.

whyCorrect: "The caster tips the surplus back out after a few minutes" and "a wall of even thickness is left standing in the mould" are each complete sentences, and no conjunction joins them. A semicolon is the correct link.

whyWrong.A: Without punctuation, "after a few minutes a wall" reads as one phrase and the second clause has no visible starting point.
whyWrong.B: A colon does not take a following and, and what comes after here is a second clause, not an explanation or list the colon can introduce.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: Strip out the phrase set off by commas and the sentence is "The inspector ... needs to work quickly." A phrase beginning together with is not part of the subject and does not make it plural, so the singular verb is required.

whyWrong.B: Needing is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb — a fragment.
whyWrong.C: Besides being plural, the present perfect puts the need in the past, which clashes with the general rule the passage is stating.
whyWrong.D: Need is plural and agrees with "volunteers," the noun inside the interrupting phrase, rather than with the actual subject.

commonMistakes: Treating together with, along with, or as well as as if it were and.

whyCorrect: With neither ... nor, the verb agrees with whichever subject sits closer to it. Here that is "the two volunteers," which is plural, so the plural present-tense verb is right.

whyWrong.A: Has been is singular and also shifts to the present perfect, which does not fit the ongoing situation described.
whyWrong.B: Is agrees with "archivist," the more distant subject, not with the nearer plural one.
whyWrong.D: Was is both singular and past, and the surrounding sentences describe the present state of the records.

whyCorrect: The men lifted out the straw and discovered damage that had already happened — the cracking occurred "somewhere between the bench and the carrier's cart," before the crate was opened. An event completed before another past event takes the past perfect.

whyWrong.B: Will crack places the damage in the future, but the men are looking at plates that are already broken.
whyWrong.C: Are cracking describes something happening right now and continuously, which cannot be what they found in a crate.
whyWrong.D: The simple present states a general habit, as if plates crack routinely, rather than reporting this one shipment.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says Mediterranean soda glass survives two thousand years almost unchanged; the second says northern potash glass weathers into a destructive crust. Two glassmaking traditions with opposite outcomes calls for a transition marking contrast.

whyWrong.B: In other words signals a restatement, but the second sentence gives new and opposite information, not the same point rephrased.
whyWrong.C: Nevertheless concedes something despite the first statement; there is no concession here, just a straight comparison of two cases.
whyWrong.D: As a result claims the northern glass decays because Mediterranean glass survives, which is not a causal relationship at all.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a problem and its cause: rounded quarry stone rolls away once undercut. The second gives the engineering response — interlocking concrete units that grip harder as the sea works on them. The second follows from the first as a remedy, so a cause-and-effect transition is needed.

whyWrong.A: Similarly would say the concrete units behave like the loose boulders, but they behave in the opposite way.
whyWrong.B: In fact intensifies or confirms the preceding claim; the second sentence changes the subject to a different design instead.
whyWrong.D: Nevertheless marks a contrast against expectation, but modern armouring is exactly what the stated problem would lead you to expect.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences establish a cost: cargo from an anchored ship was handled and paid for twice. The sentence after the blank states the consequence — a port with deep-water berths was cheaper than its rivals even before it was any faster. That is a result, so the transition must signal effect.

whyWrong.A: By contrast sets two things against each other, but the cheaper port is the outcome of the double handling, not its opposite.
whyWrong.B: Nevertheless implies the price advantage came despite the double handling, when it came because of it.
whyWrong.C: For example would make the whole conclusion about undercutting rivals into an instance of double handling, which it is not.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain why the heat judgement matters so much, which means the sentence has to connect the stakes to the practice. Only one option supplies both: the impression is irreversible and the cover is ruined if the heat is wrong, so the finisher tests the tool by sound against a damp sponge first.

whyWrong.A: The glaire adhesive is accurate from the notes but explains what the gold sticks to, not why heat control is critical.
whyWrong.C: This gives the testing method alone, with no statement of what is at risk, so it never answers "why does it matter."
whyWrong.D: This is background on what finishing is; it mentions heated tools without any consequence attached.

tips: When the goal says "explain why," pick the option that pairs a fact with a consequence — a single note restated on its own almost never does the job.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain survival, so the sentence has to link a cause — inaccessibility — to the effect — undisturbed contents. Only one option combines the two notes that do that work: the least accessible ledges can be reached only by rope from above, and it is exactly those tombs that have been found intact.

whyWrong.A: This is background on Chachapoya burial practice and says nothing about why any tomb escaped looting.
whyWrong.B: The painted house-like tombs at Revash describe appearance, which is unrelated to survival.
whyWrong.C: This explains why the accessible tombs were emptied, the opposite half of the picture, and never accounts for the ones that survived.

whyCorrect: The goal names one thing: what the 1976 passage was meant to demonstrate. The relevant notes are the canoe's purpose — testing whether long Pacific passages could be sailed without instruments — and the fact that no compass, chart or clock was aboard. The sentence that states the intention and the conditions together is the only one that answers the question asked.

whyWrong.A: The launch date and hull type are true but describe the vessel, not the purpose of the voyage.
whyWrong.C: Piailug's role and his later teaching are about who navigated and what followed, not about what the passage was designed to show.
whyWrong.D: This is a bare itinerary — launched in 1975, arrived in 1976 — with no mention of instruments or of anything being tested.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets up a single property doing two jobs: the same feature that made the ink valuable to a records office also made it a problem. That feature is the ink biting into the fibre, so an error cannot be washed out and must be scraped away with the parchment. The blank needs a word for a mark that cannot be undone.

whyWrong.A: Cost never comes up; the passage is about how the ink bonds to the page.
whyWrong.B: Fashion is not what a chancery values, and nothing in the text concerns taste.
whyWrong.D: Illegible contradicts the passage — the ink's blackness and permanence are precisely what make it readable.

whyCorrect: The passage defines the one condition that defeated earlier materials: setting under water. Smeaton's clay-bearing lime hardens while submerged, so in exactly that condition his mortar could be relied on. The blank needs a word meaning it can be counted on.

whyWrong.A: The passage never compares prices; the trials were about which limestone set under water.
whyWrong.B: Visibility is irrelevant to mortar in a submerged foundation.
whyWrong.C: Decoration has no bearing on a lighthouse mortar chosen for its behaviour in sea water.

whyCorrect: The sentence describes a moraine with no document recording it and no wood left to date, so ordinarily there would be no way at all to get an age. Lichen measurement supplies a figure in that situation, meaning the figure would otherwise not exist to be had.

whyWrong.A: Disputed would mean rival dates are argued over, but the problem stated is that there is no other source of a date at all.
whyWrong.B: Costly implies the figure could still be obtained by spending more; the passage rules out the alternative methods entirely, not on grounds of expense.
whyWrong.C: Arbitrary would describe a figure chosen at random, whereas the passage says none could be produced by other means.

whyCorrect: The unsized sheet "drinks up" ink so a line spreads into a blot; the gelatine bath fills the gaps between fibres so ink sits on the surface instead. The change is in how much liquid the sheet takes in, and the final sentence says sizing changes this rather than the fibre itself.

whyWrong.A: Opacity is about how much light passes through, which the passage never raises.
whyWrong.C: Durability would mean resistance to wear or tearing; sizing here is described purely in terms of ink behaviour.
whyWrong.D: Expense is not a property of the sheet that gelatine alters in the way the sentence describes.

whyCorrect: The sentence pairs translucency with a second quality, and the passage gives that second quality twice: bone-ash porcelain chips less readily than continental hard paste, and a crate of it survived carriage. Both point to resistance to damage.

whyWrong.A: Porous is the opposite of what a vitrified, light-passing porcelain body is, and porosity is never mentioned.
whyWrong.C: Weight is not discussed, and heaviness would not explain why crates arrived unbroken.
whyWrong.D: Coarse contradicts the description of a material that looked like porcelain on the table.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the lock flight and its cost in water, the underlined sentence describes the inclined plane, and the last sentence reports what that design buys — water spent only on topping up, and twenty minutes instead of half a day. The underlined sentence introduces the arrangement whose benefits immediately follow.

whyWrong.B: The text never explains why locks are grouped into flights; it only notes that they are.
whyWrong.C: No drawback of the inclined plane is admitted anywhere; every consequence given is favourable.
whyWrong.D: Construction cost is not mentioned; the savings described are in water and time.

whyCorrect: Track the four sentences. The first makes a claim — the song is mostly other birds' songs; the second supports it with recordings of a dozen species; the third explains that young males copy older males; the fourth draws the consequence, that a phrase outlasts the bird that supplied it. That is claim, evidence, then consequence.

whyWrong.A: There is only one account of the song here; no competing explanation is raised or rejected.
whyWrong.B: No movement of a species between regions is described — a phrase persists in one district, but the birds do not spread.
whyWrong.C: The text says the recordings carry a dozen species but never ranks or lists them by frequency.

whyCorrect: The text says colonies collapse with "far more damage than the feeding alone accounts for" and then supplies the reason: the feeding wound lets viruses in, and the mite carries them from bee to bee. The closing line — the beekeeper is watching a vector rather than a parasite — states the same point. The main idea is that transmission, not feeding, does most of the harm.

whyWrong.A: The passage says the opposite: the viruses sit at low levels in untroubled colonies, so they are present without mites.
whyWrong.B: The text treats a mite count as informative — it is a measure of virus spread — not as useless.
whyWrong.D: The first sentence says the mite feeds on the developing bee in its cell and on the emerged adult.

whyCorrect: The last sentence states the point directly: the alternation of hard night frost and strong daytime sun "belongs to the altitude," so the food is a product of the plateau. Everything before it describes the freeze-tread-thaw cycle that those conditions make possible.

whyWrong.A: No fire is mentioned; the drying is done by frost, treading and sun.
whyWrong.B: The passage argues the reverse — the technique could not have been carried up from the lowlands because the conditions it needs exist only high up.
whyWrong.D: The text says the tubers keep for years in a dry store, not a single season.

whyCorrect: Kerrigan's claim has two parts: the real difficulty is the recurring cost of keeping the channel clear, and it is not the pier's length. The quotation must dismiss building work and put the emphasis on annual expenditure. The line about sand returning every winter, with clearing costs exceeding building costs for eleven years running, does both.

whyWrong.A: This describes what the extension would achieve and so supports the pier-length framing Kerrigan says the report was warning against.
whyWrong.B: The soundness of the existing masonry is a structural finding with no bearing on annual dredging costs.
whyWrong.C: More coasting vessels speaks to demand for the harbour, not to the expense of maintaining its channel.

whyCorrect: The blank has to name the apiary with the largest gap between the two columns, so subtract at each: Ashgrove 3.7, Braemore 4.6, Cairnhead 2.2, Dunmore 5.2. Dunmore's 22.3 against 17.1 is the widest difference, and the option that states both figures is the one that shows it.

whyWrong.A: Ashgrove's 20.9 is a single figure with no sealed value beside it, and its gap of 3.7 is not the widest.
whyWrong.C: Cairnhead has the smallest gap of the four, and 19.8 is also the one unsealed reading below twenty per cent.
whyWrong.D: Braemore's sealed comb is indeed the driest at 16.8, but the sentence asks for the widest sealed-to-unsealed difference, and Braemore's 4.6 is smaller than Dunmore's 5.2.

commonMistakes: Picking the single largest or smallest number in a column when the sentence actually asks for the largest difference between two columns.

whyCorrect: Ostrander has to beat one specific rival explanation: that families took high plots because population pressure left them nothing better. Evidence that the households doing this were among the wealthiest, and that they took up outlying plots while valley-floor land was still free, removes the pressure explanation and leaves deliberate choice.

whyWrong.B: Long journeys between plots show the arrangement was costly, which if anything makes it look like a burden rather than a deliberate strategy.
whyWrong.C: That maize grows only below a certain altitude explains why the zones differ but says nothing about why households chose to hold plots in several of them.
whyWrong.D: Plots on both slopes of one valley involve no difference in climate zone, so this does not bear on the multiple-climates claim.

tips: For support questions, ask what the competing explanation is and pick the finding that rules it out.

whyCorrect: The sail works with the wind abeam or behind and cannot be driven into a headwind, and the islands' sailing directions say to wait out a season rather than beat against it. If you must wait for the wind to change, the wind decides when you sail.

whyWrong.A: Hull length is never mentioned; the constraint described is the sail's inability to work to windward.
whyWrong.B: Paddlers appear nowhere in the text, which is about sailing performance.
whyWrong.D: This contradicts the passage outright — wind direction is precisely what limits when the canoe can go.

whyCorrect: Two facts combine. Cloud scatters ultraviolet without absorbing much of it, so a grey day is not protective; and the injury appears only some hours after the exposure. A party out all day therefore cannot judge the damage until hours later.

whyWrong.A: The passage explicitly says overcast gives little protection because cloud scatters the light through.
whyWrong.B: This contradicts the stated delay — the injury shows up hours afterwards, not within minutes.
whyWrong.C: Snow reflects most of the ultraviolet falling on it, so the traveller takes it from below as well as from above.

whyCorrect: "An experienced traveller in the Canadian Arctic" is an appositive describing Amundsen, and it is already opened with a comma after his name. A pair of commas has to close as well as open, so a comma belongs after Arctic, just before the verb took.

whyWrong.A: A colon cannot sit between a subject's modifier and its verb; it also promises an explanation or list that does not follow.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation the appositive is left half-enclosed — opened by a comma and never closed.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "took dogs from the outset and planned to kill the weaker ones" has no subject of its own.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that a comma opening a nonessential phrase must be matched by a comma closing it.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with a subordinate clause beginning Because and running to "in Egypt"; the main clause is "the chronology ... had to be carried back." An introductory subordinate clause is separated from the main clause by a comma.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but the Because clause cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete clause; the Because clause is a fragment on its own.
whyWrong.D: Adding and leaves the sentence with no main clause at all — both halves become subordinate to Because.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with a Because clause that ends at "a year," and the main clause follows: "the builders laid a bed of broken stone ...". An introductory subordinate clause is set off from the main clause with a comma.

whyWrong.A: A colon has to follow a complete sentence, and the Because clause cannot stand on its own.
whyWrong.B: With and, both halves fall under Because and the sentence never reaches a main clause — a fragment.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon links two independent clauses; the opening clause here is dependent.

whyCorrect: "Agitate the cloth in hot water and the scales lock against one another and will not come apart" is one complete sentence; "the cloth shrinks, thickens and stops fraying at a cut edge" is another. With no conjunction between them, a semicolon does the joining.

whyWrong.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: Unpunctuated, "come apart the cloth shrinks" runs the two clauses into one another with no boundary.
whyWrong.D: A colon is not used with a following and, and what follows is a second clause rather than an explanation or list.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The average weight," which is singular; "of the eight colonies on the moorland site" is a prepositional phrase and cannot control the verb. "This year" places the statement in the present, so the singular present-tense verb is correct.

whyWrong.A: Have been is plural and shifts into the present perfect, which does not match the single seasonal figure being reported.
whyWrong.B: Are agrees with "colonies" inside the prepositional phrase rather than with "average."
whyWrong.C: Were is both plural and past, clashing with "this year."

commonMistakes: Letting a plural noun inside an of phrase set the verb instead of the real subject.

whyCorrect: The three actions share the helping verb will: the binder will pull the book apart, resew the sections, and lace the boards back on. Parallel structure requires the same bare form in each item of the list.

whyWrong.A: Laces is a finite present-tense form that cannot follow will, and it breaks the pattern set by pull and resew.
whyWrong.C: To lace introduces an infinitive that does not match the other two items after will.
whyWrong.D: Lacing is a participle, so the third item stops being a verb the way the first two are.

whyCorrect: The comparison is between two yellows, not between a yellow and a house, so the second half needs a pronoun standing in for "the yellow" plus the same participial phrase. Singular that matches the singular noun it replaces: the yellow struck in the eastern house is deeper than that struck in the western one.

whyWrong.A: They struck is plural and turns the houses into the subject, so the sentence compares a colour with an action.
whyWrong.B: This compares a yellow with a building — an illogical comparison, since the western house itself is not deeper than a colour.
whyWrong.D: Those is plural, but the thing being compared, "the yellow," is singular.

whyCorrect: Pre-1800 rag paper stays supple and folds without cracking; 1890 wood-pulp paper snaps at the fold. The two sentences describe opposite outcomes for two kinds of paper, so the transition has to mark contrast.

whyWrong.A: Likewise claims the second case behaves the same way as the first, but it behaves in the opposite way.
whyWrong.C: Therefore would make the brittleness of 1890 paper a consequence of rag paper's suppleness, which is not a causal link.
whyWrong.D: In short announces a summary, and the second sentence adds a new and contrasting case.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states that fading depends on total lifetime light exposure and is never recovered. The second describes what galleries do about it — low light, short exhibitions, long spells in the dark. Those practices follow from the fact stated, so the transition must show effect.

whyWrong.B: Nevertheless would mark the gallery's caution as surprising given the fading, when it is exactly the expected response.
whyWrong.C: By contrast sets two things against each other; the second sentence agrees with and acts on the first.
whyWrong.D: For example would present gallery practice as an instance of fading, but it is a response to fading, not a case of it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes the ridges a burden — a day spent hauling sledges over them. The second turns that round: the same ridges let a driver hold a course when the sun is hidden. A benefit offered despite the drawback just described calls for a concessive transition.

whyWrong.A: As a result would make the navigational use a consequence of the hard hauling, but the two are opposed benefits and costs of the same feature.
whyWrong.B: In other words signals a restatement, and the second sentence says something new and different.
whyWrong.D: For instance would offer navigation as an example of the labour described, which it is not.

whyCorrect: The goal is the difficulty the painter faced while working with smalt, and the notes contain a genuine bind: coarse particles keep the blue strong but will not disperse and leave gritty paint, while grinding finer smooths the paint and kills the colour. Stating both horns of that choice is what explains the difficulty.

whyWrong.A: Cheapness is smalt's advantage, not the problem the painter had to solve.
whyWrong.B: This defines what smalt is and names no difficulty at all.
whyWrong.D: The grey discoloration happens over time, long after the picture is finished, so it is not a difficulty in working the paint.

whyCorrect: To explain a purpose you need the constraint and the fix in one sentence. The gates open only at level water, which limits access to a short window each day; the half-tide basin sits in front of the dock and lengthens that window. Only one option puts the limitation and the remedy together.

whyWrong.B: This says the basin was built and where, but not what problem it solved.
whyWrong.C: Tidal harbours and ships taking the ground are background about the alternative arrangement, not the basin's purpose.
whyWrong.D: This gives the constraint alone, with no mention of the basin or what it achieved.

whyCorrect: The goal is a design decision that cut the load carried. Two notes combine into that: the upper part of each pier was built hollow, and a hollow pier weighs far less than a solid one of the same size. Pairing the decision with its weight saving is what emphasises the point.

whyWrong.B: The cast-iron trough bedded in flannel and lead is a construction detail about watertightness, not about reducing weight.
whyWrong.C: Naming the designers says nothing about any decision that lightened the structure.
whyWrong.D: Height and completion date are background facts with no bearing on load.

whyCorrect: The passage defines the word before using it: a colour that comes through a month in a south-facing window and six washes "without shifting" is fast. The sense required is therefore resistance to change — the colour is held firmly in place.

whyWrong.A: The speed sense has nothing to do with light exposure or laundering; nothing in the passage moves.
whyWrong.C: The abstaining-from-food sense is unrelated to cloth or dye.
whyWrong.D: The clock sense would describe a watch running ahead, which cannot apply to a colour.

tips: When a passage sets up a test and then labels the result, the label means whatever passing that test demonstrates.

whyCorrect: The sentence rules out food and building material, so the blank must name the function actually described: the bees smear the resin over cracks and rough surfaces, and it closes draughts, stiffens joints and suppresses microbes on shared surfaces. All of that is the work of a substance that seals gaps and coats surfaces.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text says the material communicates anything between bees; every effect listed is physical.
whyWrong.C: A reserve is something stored for later use, which is close to the "food" sense the sentence explicitly excludes.
whyWrong.D: Fuel would be consumed for energy, but the propolis stays in place doing its work.

whyCorrect: The sentence balances two halves: the treatment leaves the cotton chemically unchanged but does something to its appearance. The passage says the fibre rounds out, takes dye more readily and reflects light along its length instead of scattering it — a visible change. The blank needs a word meaning it changes the look completely.

whyWrong.A: Conceals would mean hiding the appearance, but the point is that the appearance itself is altered and on show.
whyWrong.B: Predicts makes no sense of a physical treatment; nothing is being forecast.
whyWrong.C: Preserves repeats the first half of the contrast instead of completing it — the sentence needs the appearance to change, not stay the same.

whyCorrect: The mordant is taken up by the fibre beforehand and forms a link that the dye attaches to afterwards, and it adds almost no colour itself. Its entire role is to get the fibre ready for the dye that follows.

whyWrong.A: Decorative is ruled out by the sentence itself, which says the mordant contributes almost no colour.
whyWrong.B: Accidental would make the effect unintended, but the dyer applies the mordant deliberately and in advance.
whyWrong.D: Temporary contradicts the passage — the mordant is what makes the colour permanent rather than washing out.

whyCorrect: The problem stated is ash and flame striking the glaze and flecking the ware. The fireclay box "take[s] up the heat but keep[s] everything else out," so it stands between the pot and the fire. The blank needs a word for something that protects.

whyWrong.B: A measure would record or gauge something; the box does no measuring.
whyWrong.C: Decoration is the opposite of its purpose, and the sentence says the box is no part of the pot.
whyWrong.D: A mould gives a piece its shape, but the pot is already formed before it goes into the box.

whyCorrect: Everything in the text builds to the last two sentences: the knot spacing and the glass are chosen so that the raw count is the speed in sea miles an hour, and nothing has to be calculated on deck. The purpose is to show how a simple device converts a physical observation straight into a usable number.

whyWrong.B: No later instrument is mentioned, so no comparison of accuracy is made.
whyWrong.C: The sand glass appears only as part of the timing; how glasses were made is never discussed.
whyWrong.D: The sea mile is used as the unit the count comes out in, but the text does not trace how it came to be adopted.

whyCorrect: The text first lays out what the vessels show — the same face at sites a hundred kilometres apart, ageing between examples, with scars and injuries modelled as carefully as the headdresses — and then names the open question about whether these are portraits or standard types. Describing the evidence and the debate it provokes is the purpose.

whyWrong.A: The text says the question is argued over and only that a repertoire alone is hard to square with the evidence; it stops short of claiming potters worked exclusively from live sitters.
whyWrong.B: No neighbouring culture's pottery is brought in for comparison.
whyWrong.D: The stirrup spout is mentioned in passing as a vessel form; how it was made is never explained.

whyCorrect: Three facts point the same way: a bird that hears a tutor copies it and its song freezes by about ninety days; a bird kept in silence during that stretch sings, but never settles on a normal song; and a model supplied after the window has closed makes almost no difference. Together they say the learning happens inside a limited early period.

whyWrong.B: The passage says silence-raised birds do sing as adults — their song is just abnormal and unstable.
whyWrong.C: Learning is not lifelong here; after about ninety days the song stops changing and a new model has little effect.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the text describes seasonal reworking of adult song; the point is that adult song is fixed.

whyCorrect: The last sentence carries the idea: an entrepot can prosper while the region behind it stays poor, and it is hurt when a trade route bypasses it rather than when local harvests fail. Its income comes from handling goods in transit, so what matters is the traffic passing through, not local demand.

whyWrong.A: The text says the opposite — an entrepot suffers from being bypassed, not from its neighbours' bad harvests.
whyWrong.C: The passage states the entrepot earns from the handling rather than from the sale, and the goods were never meant for its own market.
whyWrong.D: No comparison of overall profitability is made; the text contrasts what each type of port depends on.

whyCorrect: Ibarra's claim is about which components of the wood disappear: brown rot removes cellulose and leaves lignin, white rot removes both. Support therefore has to be a measurement of the two fractions in each kind of decayed timber, which is exactly what the chemical analysis provides.

whyWrong.A: Crumbling shows the timber is weakened, but weakness is consistent with either fungus removing either component.
whyWrong.B: A shared moisture requirement applies equally to both fungi and so distinguishes nothing.
whyWrong.D: Which tree species each fungus prefers is about distribution, not about what it digests.

tips: A support question wants evidence about the exact quantity the claim is about — here the amounts of cellulose and lignin left behind.

whyCorrect: Nowicka's claim has two halves, and both need support: song is picked up from the neighbours a male settles among, and the boundary is not maintained by reluctance to interbreed. Ringed birds that moved across the line and sing their new valley's version cover the first, and cross-boundary pairings being as common as within-valley ones rules out the breeding barrier.

whyWrong.A: How the two versions differ acoustically describes the songs, not how they are acquired or why the line holds.
whyWrong.B: A ridge birds seldom cross in winter suggests a physical barrier, which is closer to the rival explanation than to Nowicka's.
whyWrong.C: Stronger responses to the local version show the birds tell the dialects apart; that is equally consistent with a mating barrier.

whyCorrect: The blank names the pigment that had moved furthest at the 200-hour reading, so compare that column only: 0.9, 1.2, 3.9 and 6.8. Brazilwood lake's 6.8 is the largest, and the option that cites it and follows it to 14.2 units at 600 hours completes the sentence correctly.

whyWrong.A: Madder lake moved only 1.2 units at 200 hours, one of the two pigments still below the visible threshold at 600.
whyWrong.B: Kermes lake is the least changed of the four, the opposite of what the sentence asks for.
whyWrong.D: Weld lake's 3.9 units is second to brazilwood's 6.8 at the 200-hour mark.

whyCorrect: The mycelium fruits at its advancing edge and cannot grow back into ground it has already stripped, so where two rings meet, the section of each arc facing the other has nowhere to go. Growth continues everywhere else, so the two circles stop against each other and the shared boundary is left as a straight line.

whyWrong.B: Merging into one larger circle would require growth across the exhausted ground between them, which the passage rules out.
whyWrong.C: Growing back towards the centre means re-entering ground the fungus has already exhausted — precisely what it cannot do.
whyWrong.D: Heavier fruiting at the contact line contradicts the fact that this is where neither ring can advance.

whyCorrect: The passage gives the reaction three ingredients: chloride in the corrosion layer, copper, and damp air. Brushing removes only the powder and leaves the chloride underneath. Fresh powder two years after cleaning therefore means both the chloride is still there and the room is damp enough for the reaction to keep running.

whyWrong.B: Salty burial is exactly how the chloride got into the object, so fresh powder points towards that history, not away from it.
whyWrong.C: The text says the powder eats further into the metal as it forms, so it is destructive rather than protective.
whyWrong.D: Copper is one of the reactants, so the powder's appearance shows copper is present.

whyCorrect: "Engineers narrow the mouth between two low walls so that the same volume of water runs through a smaller section" and "the current that results scours the channel deeper than the river would ever have run of its own accord" are both complete sentences. Joining two independent clauses with and requires a comma before the conjunction.

whyWrong.A: Without the comma, the reader first takes "a smaller section and the current" as a compound object of through and has to reparse the sentence.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon already joins independent clauses on its own; adding and after it is not standard.
whyWrong.D: A colon introduces an explanation or list directly and is never followed by a coordinating conjunction.

whyCorrect: "Nothing in it is meant to sit through a season" is complete, and so is "Goods that wait on a market are sent inland to a warehouse, where the land costs less." With no conjunction available in any option that also punctuates correctly, the full stop is the one choice that separates the two clauses properly.

whyWrong.A: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon does the joining by itself; following it with and is not standard punctuation.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation at all, "a season goods that wait" runs the clauses together and reads as a single garbled phrase.

whyCorrect: "A songbird's voice box sits where the windpipe divides in two, and a set of vibrating membranes is carried on each branch" is a complete sentence. What follows is a list of the consequences — two sources of sound, two sets of muscles, a bird able to sing two lines at once — and a colon after a complete clause is what introduces such a list.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, and the list that follows has no verb of its own.
whyWrong.B: A comma plus and also demands a full second clause; the string of noun phrases after it is not one.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation, "on each branch two sources of sound" runs the list straight into the clause with nothing to mark where it begins.

whyCorrect: The list of details — the fall of a sleeve, the modelling of a cheek, the depth of a shadow — is an interruption inserted between the subject "Everything the painter put into that cartoon" and its verb "has." An interruption opened with a dash must be closed with a matching dash.

whyWrong.B: A comma cannot close a parenthesis that a dash opened; the punctuation marks have to match.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon would end a clause, but the subject has not yet reached its verb, so the first part is not a clause.
whyWrong.D: A colon cannot close the dashed insertion, and there is no complete clause in front of it to introduce anything.

commonMistakes: Mixing punctuation marks at the two ends of a nonessential element — a dash must be answered by a dash, a comma by a comma.

whyCorrect: "Running low on fuel on the return" is a modifier with no subject of its own, so whatever noun opens the main clause is taken as the thing running low on fuel. Only the party can be running low on fuel, so the main clause has to begin with the party.

whyWrong.A: This makes "an hour before dark" the thing running low on fuel — a dangling modifier.
whyWrong.B: Here the sighting itself is running low on fuel, which is equally impossible.
whyWrong.C: The flags become the subject, so the sentence says the flags were running low on fuel.

tips: After an opening -ing phrase, check the very next noun: it must be the one performing that action.

whyCorrect: The sentence is inverted — the place phrase comes first and the subject follows the verb. The subject is "three boxes of lichen-dyed wool," which is plural, so the verb must be plural too.

whyWrong.A: Is is singular and appears to agree with "shelf" or "samples" in the opening phrase, neither of which is the subject.
whyWrong.B: Sits is also singular, so it fails to agree with the plural "three boxes."
whyWrong.D: Was is singular and past, while the surrounding sentences describe the store's present arrangement.

whyCorrect: There are two past times here: the mapping under closed canopy four years before, and the later comparison of the two image sets. The earlier of two past events takes the past perfect, so had mapped is required.

whyWrong.A: The present perfect links the mapping to the present rather than placing it before another past event, and it clashes with "four years earlier."
whyWrong.C: Will map puts the mapping in the future, but it happened before the 2023 fire.
whyWrong.D: The simple present describes a habitual or current action, not a completed survey four years back.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the benefit of singing higher in traffic — the song clears the low rumble. The second gives the cost: a higher song carries less far. A drawback set against a benefit just stated calls for a contrastive transition.

whyWrong.A: Therefore would make the loss of range a consequence of escaping the rumble rather than a price paid against it.
whyWrong.B: Likewise claims the second point runs parallel to the first, but the two pull in opposite directions.
whyWrong.C: For instance would offer the shorter range as an example of clearing the rumble, which it is not.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states the danger: damaged manioc root releases cyanide and can kill if eaten raw. The second describes the grating, squeezing and hard boiling that answer that danger. The processing follows from the hazard, so the transition must signal consequence.

whyWrong.A: By contrast sets the processing against the toxicity, but the processing exists because of the toxicity.
whyWrong.B: Even so would mark the processing as happening despite the danger, when it is a response to it.
whyWrong.C: Instead needs a rejected alternative in the first sentence, and there is none — poisoning is not an option someone chose against.

whyCorrect: The first sentence explains that comb fixed to the skep's walls has to be cut away before the colony can be seen. The second states what followed from that: inspection destroyed what was inspected, and the crop was taken by killing the bees. The relationship is cause to consequence.

whyWrong.A: For example would make destructive inspection an instance of comb being attached to the walls, but it is the result of that arrangement.
whyWrong.C: Nevertheless marks something happening against expectation, and this is exactly what the fixed comb would lead you to expect.
whyWrong.D: By contrast requires two things set against each other; the second sentence agrees with and extends the first.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for the evidence that the markings guide bees, which means the sentence must connect what the markings do with what happens when they are removed. Two notes supply that: the markings converge on the nectar, and masking them cuts the number and length of bee visits.

whyWrong.A: That bees see ultraviolet and people do not explains why the markings are invisible to us — background, not evidence of guidance.
whyWrong.B: The bare existence of ultraviolet markings says nothing about their effect on bees.
whyWrong.C: The filter photograph shows the markings can be made visible; it demonstrates a technique, not a behavioural effect.

whyCorrect: To show the colour is made rather than extracted, the sentence must contrast the lichen before and after treatment. The notes give exactly that pair: no purple is present in the raw lichen, and the colour appears only after weeks in ammoniacal liquor.

whyWrong.B: This states where the dye comes from, which if anything suggests the purple was in the lichen all along.
whyWrong.C: Fading and use on cheap cloth concern the dye's quality and market, not how the colour arises.
whyWrong.D: Dyeing without a mordant is about how the colour attaches to wool, not about how it is created.

whyCorrect: Explaining how the shape protected the ship needs the mechanism and its result. The rounded hull with no sharp turn of bilge gives closing ice nothing to grip, so the pressure lifts the vessel instead of crushing it, and the three undamaged years in the pack show it worked.

whyWrong.A: The dates of the drift record what happened without saying anything about the hull.
whyWrong.B: This describes the shape alone, leaving out why that shape mattered when the ice closed.
whyWrong.D: The lost sailing quality is the design's cost, the opposite of an explanation of its protective effect.

whyCorrect: The passage is entirely about texture: cutting fine and pressing hard gives a paste that slices without crumbling, while doing neither gives one that spreads under a knife. The underlined word names the quality those decisions aim at, which is the cheese's consistency.

whyWrong.A: The main-part-of-a-text sense needs a written work, and there is none.
whyWrong.B: The organised-group sense cannot be what a cheesemaker adjusts by cutting curd.
whyWrong.D: A shapeless quantity of matter would describe an amount of stuff, but the passage is about firmness against spreadability, not quantity.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts the blank with "a vote thrown away," so it needs the word for what actually happens to those ballots: when the weakest candidate is eliminated, the ballots pass to each voter's next name. The vote moves rather than being discarded.

whyWrong.A: Confidentiality concerns the secret ballot and is never at issue in the counting procedure described.
whyWrong.B: Provisional would suggest the preference is only tentative, but the vote is fully counted — it simply moves to a later name when the first is eliminated.
whyWrong.C: Irrelevant is a synonym for the thing the sentence contrasts the blank with, so it makes the sentence contradict itself.

whyCorrect: The two cases differ in how height is gained: rushing up from a four-thousand-metre base makes people ill, while carrying loads high and sleeping low gains height slowly and lets the body adjust. The sentence sets the blank against "a matter of pace," so it needs a word for success achieved in small stages.

whyWrong.B: Accidental would deny any method at all, but the passage describes a deliberate and effective one.
whyWrong.C: Effortless contradicts a description of repeated load-carrying up and down a mountain.
whyWrong.D: Competitive introduces rivalry between climbers, which the passage never mentions.

whyCorrect: The passage says the building is separated from the earthquake rather than braced against it, and that the bearings are soft enough sideways for the ground to move a foot while the structure sways slowly above. The blank must describe a connection that deliberately allows that relative movement.

whyWrong.B: Watertightness has nothing to do with the sideways movement the bearings permit.
whyWrong.C: The bearings are structural, and the passage assigns them no visual role.
whyWrong.D: Rigid is the opposite of what is described — a stiff connection would carry the ground's motion straight into the building.

whyCorrect: The underlined word takes the modifier "even-aged" and is contrasted with "one holding trees of many ages," so it names a body of trees on a parcel. That is the forestry sense: the trees growing together on a given site.

whyWrong.A: A support or piece of furniture cannot be planted after a clearance or thinned on a schedule.
whyWrong.C: An opinion cannot be even-aged or hold trees of many ages.
whyWrong.D: A halt in growth would make "an even-aged halt planted after a clearance" nonsense.

whyCorrect: The text has two movements. First the danger: because one box works both signals and points, a signalman can clear a route while the far points still lie for another. Then the fix: levers locked to one another in a frame so a signal cannot be pulled off unless the route is set and locked. Purpose is to lay out the hazard and its mechanical solution.

whyWrong.B: Electrical systems are never mentioned, so no comparison is made with them.
whyWrong.C: The mechanics of moving points are assumed, not explained; the text is about the interlocking between levers.
whyWrong.D: No individual engineer is named or followed.

whyCorrect: The text follows one sequence: an odd smear of signal, resolved into pulses of remarkable regularity, then months of eliminating radar, car ignitions and an alien message, ending with a natural explanation — a spinning collapsed star. That is an account of an unexplained signal being traced to its source.

whyWrong.B: Optical surveys are not mentioned, so nothing is claimed about which kind is more productive.
whyWrong.C: The spin is stated as part of the explanation; how the star came to spin so fast is never addressed.
whyWrong.D: Instruments appear only as the high-speed recordings that resolved the pulses, not as the subject of the text.

whyCorrect: The passage says the holes form "while the wheel sat in a warm room" and that cold-ripened wheels "contain the same bacterium and stay solid." Since the organism is present either way, the missing ingredient in the cold wheels is the warmth that lets it work.

whyWrong.A: The lactic acid comes from the starter cultures, which are used in both cases; the text never says cold ripening removes it.
whyWrong.B: The last sentence states directly that cold-ripened wheels contain the same bacterium.
whyWrong.D: This inverts the explanation — elasticity is what lets the paste stretch around a bubble instead of cracking, so more elasticity would help holes form, not prevent them.

whyCorrect: The text explicitly rules out simple neglect by pointing to embryos that start an eye and then dismantle it — an active process. It then gives the reason: eyes are expensive to build and run and return nothing in permanent darkness. The main idea is that the loss reflects that cost.

whyWrong.A: No relationship between cave fish and cave crayfish is claimed; they are two examples of the same pattern.
whyWrong.B: Cave-mouth populations are given as the contrast case that keeps its eyes; the text makes no prediction about them.
whyWrong.C: The passage denies exactly this — the embryo does form eye tissue, and the tissue is then broken down, which is not a failure to develop.

whyCorrect: The claim is that the substitutions force two unlike activities to be seen as one, so the quotation has to sustain a single figure across both. Sowing the sea-field with oars, reaping a harvest of salt, and setting that against the ploughman's tillage runs seafaring and farming together throughout.

whyWrong.B: This is a dating note about when the verse was made and contains no figure at all.
whyWrong.C: This states the convention from outside, as a description of what poets do, rather than doing it.
whyWrong.D: "Wave-horse" is a single substitution used as a label for a ship; it never brings two activities into one frame.

whyCorrect: Bergström has to separate two explanations that arrived at the same moment: the quota and the wetter years. The finding that isolates one is a comparison in which the weather is the same but the policy is not — neighbouring districts on the same aquifer, with the same wet years but no metering, kept losing water table at the old rate.

whyWrong.A: Above-average rainfall strengthens the rival explanation she is arguing against.
whyWrong.B: Trading a quarter of the quota shows the market was used, but not that the water table's recovery came from the scheme rather than the rain.
whyWrong.C: How the aquifer recharges is background hydrology and does not distinguish between the two causes.

tips: When two causes coincide, the supporting finding is the case that holds one of them constant and varies the other.

whyCorrect: Duarte's claim is that the mechanics of the thorax, not the nerve signal rate, set the wingbeat. The decisive test changes a mechanical property and watches both variables: adding a little mass shifts the wingbeat exactly as resonance predicts while the nerve signal rate stays put.

whyWrong.A: Slower beating in cold air is expected under either account, since both muscle and mechanical properties change with temperature.
whyWrong.B: Flying in circles after wing damage is about balance and control, not about what sets the beat frequency.
whyWrong.D: A stiff thorax deformed by the muscle describes the anatomy that makes resonance possible but does not show resonance is what fixes the rate.

whyCorrect: The tolerance stated is relative: the surface must depart from a paraboloid by much less than the observing wavelength, and a big dish inevitably sags as it tips. A shorter wavelength means a tighter tolerance, so the dish must stay smaller. Centimetre work therefore allows a far bigger dish than millimetre work does.

whyWrong.B: Faintness is a sensitivity issue and would argue for a larger dish, not a smaller one; the passage's limit is about surface accuracy.
whyWrong.C: Time of day never enters the passage; the varying factor is the elevation the dish is pointed at.
whyWrong.D: Fixing the elevation removes the changing sag and so relaxes the constraint, which would allow a larger dish rather than a smaller one.

whyCorrect: Air is driven through the opening by the difference between cave temperature, near the annual mean, and outside temperature, and in August the outside is warmer, so cool cave air flows out. For that flow to be strong and steady rather than a brief puff, there must be a large body of air behind it — a substantial space beyond the crack.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the passage links airflow to running water; the driver described is a temperature difference.
whyWrong.B: Standing water is not mentioned and would not explain a sustained outward draught.
whyWrong.C: Whether a passage has been surveyed is a matter of record, not something airflow could reveal.

whyCorrect: "The throat is built for exactly that job" is a complete sentence, and what follows — pleats running from the chin to the navel and opening like a bellows — explains what that construction consists of. A colon after a complete clause is what introduces an explanation of this kind.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "that job pleats running" collides two noun phrases and leaves the sentence unreadable.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires a full clause on each side, and the pleats phrase has no finite verb of its own.
whyWrong.D: A comma plus and also needs an independent clause after it, but running and opening are participles, not main verbs.

whyCorrect: "A city standing almost on the fault, for instance" is an interruption dropped into the middle of the sentence, and it is opened with a dash. A parenthetical opened by a dash must be closed by a matching dash before the sentence resumes with "the warning arrives too late."

whyWrong.A: A semicolon would end a clause, but "Where the distance is short" is a subordinate clause still waiting for its main clause.
whyWrong.B: A colon cannot close a dashed insertion, and there is no complete clause in front of it.
whyWrong.D: A comma leaves the interruption half-enclosed, with a dash at one end and a comma at the other.

whyCorrect: "The surveyors sent west after 1785 worked instead from a system that needed no landmarks at all" is a complete sentence, and the three items that follow — a principal meridian, a base line, and six-mile townships — spell out what that system consisted of. A colon after a complete clause introduces such a list.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and the list of noun phrases is not a clause.
whyWrong.B: A comma plus and likewise requires a second full clause, which the list is not.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation the list runs into the clause and "no landmarks at all a north–south principal meridian" cannot be parsed.

whyCorrect: "A man who walked the moving logs with a pole and a pair of spiked boots" is a nonessential appositive describing the river driver, and it is already opened with a comma. The pair must be closed with a comma before the main verb broke.

whyWrong.A: Without the closing comma the appositive is never shut, and "spiked boots broke the jams apart" makes the boots the subject.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; "broke the jams apart at the head of the run and rode the loose wood down" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.D: A colon cannot separate a subject from its verb, and no list or explanation follows.

whyCorrect: The subject is Each, which is always singular; "of the four saws" is a prepositional phrase and does not control the verb. A singular subject in the present tense takes has.

whyWrong.A: Have agrees with "saws" inside the prepositional phrase rather than with the real subject.
whyWrong.C: Having is a participle, so the sentence would be left with no main verb — a fragment.
whyWrong.D: Were having is plural and past, and it also puts a permanent arrangement into a temporary past tense.

commonMistakes: Treating each of, either of, or neither of as plural because a plural noun follows of.

whyCorrect: The sentence lists what the money is for, and the first two items are infinitives: to tie the walls to the floors, to grout the rubble core. The third item must take the same form for the list to be parallel.

whyWrong.A: Having fixed is a perfect participle and puts the third item in a different form and a different time from the other two.
whyWrong.B: Fixing is a gerund, so the list mixes infinitives with an -ing form.
whyWrong.D: It fixes starts a new clause in the middle of a list, leaving the third item incompatible with the first two.

whyCorrect: With neither ... nor, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it, and that is "the two clients," which is plural. The sentence also needs a form that works with the participle signed, so the plural auxiliary is what fits.

whyWrong.A: Is is singular and cannot combine with signed to form a working verb phrase here.
whyWrong.B: Has agrees with "the guide," the more distant of the two subjects, instead of the nearer plural.
whyWrong.D: Was is singular and also produces "was signed," a passive that would make the clients the thing being signed.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a case an observatory can handle — ground transmitters, blocked by a valley wall and by cooperative neighbours. The second gives the case it cannot: signals coming straight down from satellites, with no hill in the way. The two situations are opposed, so the transition marks contrast.

whyWrong.A: For example would make satellite interference an instance of the shelter described, but it is the situation where that shelter fails.
whyWrong.B: Consequently claims satellites broadcast from overhead because observatories sit in valleys, which is not a causal link.
whyWrong.C: In addition treats the second sentence as another instance of the same point, when it undercuts the first.

whyCorrect: The first sentence lists the advantages of a single-species street: even maturing and a shared pruning cycle. The second gives the cost of that same uniformity — a disease reaching one tree reaches all of them, as happened to the elms. Advantage followed by drawback needs a contrastive transition.

whyWrong.A: For this reason would make disease spread a consequence of even pruning, but the two are opposite effects of the same planting choice.
whyWrong.C: In fact intensifies or confirms the preceding claim, and the second sentence works against it.
whyWrong.D: Likewise presents the second point as parallel to the first, when it is the opposing half of the picture.

whyCorrect: The first sentence credits the broad gauge with a steadier ride. The second states the penalty: at every boundary with the narrower system, wagons had to be emptied and their loads carried across. A disadvantage that stands despite the advantage just given calls for a concessive transition.

whyWrong.B: For example would make transhipment an instance of riding steadily, which it is not.
whyWrong.C: Similarly claims the second point matches the first, but one is a benefit and the other a cost.
whyWrong.D: In other words announces a restatement, and the second sentence introduces an entirely new problem.

whyCorrect: The improvement lies in the comparison: under staff and ticket the signalman could show the staff and issue a paper ticket, so the one-train rule rested on his judgement, whereas the electric instruments are wired so only one token can be out at a time. Naming both halves is what explains the advance.

whyWrong.A: This describes only the older system and gives no point of comparison.
whyWrong.B: The introduction date and the layout of the machines say nothing about what the instruments fixed.
whyWrong.D: The head-on collision risk is the background danger both systems address, not the difference between them.

whyCorrect: Explaining why the newer tests appeared means naming the defect in the old one and what replaced it. The notes supply both: a compactness score punishes districts that simply follow a coastline or a river even when honestly drawn, so the newer approach compares a map with thousands of random maps drawn under the same rules.

whyWrong.A: This describes the problem of partisan mapping in general, not why one measurement replaced another.
whyWrong.B: The formula for the compactness score explains how the old test works but not why it was found wanting.
whyWrong.D: That courts have asked about compactness is background on the old standard, with no defect and no replacement mentioned.

whyCorrect: The question asks why the old framework had to go, so the sentence needs the size of the error and the tolerance it broke. By 2020 satellite positions differed from the 1994 datum by about 1.8 metres, while self-steering machinery works to a few centimetres — an error hundreds of times the tolerance.

whyWrong.A: The date the framework was fixed is a fact about it, not a reason it failed.
whyWrong.C: This describes the replacement rather than the problem that forced it.
whyWrong.D: The plate's speed explains how the drift accumulates but stops short of saying the resulting error broke anything.

whyCorrect: The return run does more than cover the same ground: any failure to come back to the starting height reveals an error, and the size of that discrepancy is then distributed through the intermediate points. The blank must name that checking function, which the sentence contrasts with "merely repeating."

whyWrong.A: Duplicating is the very thing the sentence sets the blank against.
whyWrong.C: Nothing is put off — the return run is done immediately and produces the correction.
whyWrong.D: The return run adds a step and a correction, so it makes the work more involved, not simpler.

whyCorrect: The clause after the blank gives the reason: mounted archers on the frontier could not be fought on foot. The horses were therefore something the empire had to have, and the sentence sets the blank against "a curiosity" — an object of idle interest.

whyWrong.A: The blood-sweating story is a rumour, but the sentence asks what the horses were for the emperor, and he sent an army rather than treating them as hearsay.
whyWrong.C: A luxury is something one can do without, which contradicts a military requirement worth an army.
whyWrong.D: Tribute is something received from a subject people; here the Han had to send a force to take the horses.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the underlined word says weakly acidic rain "carries the rock away in dissolved form," and the passage insists the passages are not ground out. The word therefore names the chemical process of the limestone dissolving into the water.

whyWrong.B: A cleaning liquid is a substance rather than a process, and no such liquid appears in the passage.
whyWrong.C: Breaking rock apart by force is exactly what the text rules out with "not ground out."
whyWrong.D: The answer-to-a-problem sense would make "widened by an answer" meaningless here.

whyCorrect: The array's resolution comes from recording each dish's signal with exact timing and combining the records afterwards, so the wide aperture exists only in the processing. The sentence contrasts the blank with "built," so it needs a word for something produced by calculation.

whyWrong.A: Abandoned would say the resolution is given up, but the whole point is that it is achieved.
whyWrong.B: Nothing is bought; the passage describes a technique, not a purchase.
whyWrong.C: Estimated implies an approximation stands in for the real thing, whereas the combination genuinely delivers the resolution.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets the blank against merely blocking the sun, so it must name the second effect the passage describes: water released from the leaves consumes heat as it evaporates, which lowers the air temperature. That is why the air under the planes stands several degrees below the air over the paving.

whyWrong.A: Stirring air is movement, and the passage describes a temperature difference produced by evaporation, not by wind.
whyWrong.B: Shading is the effect the sentence explicitly says the canopy does more than.
whyWrong.D: Drying reverses the process described — the trees release water into the air rather than removing it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes that poor years show up as narrow rings, and the final sentence states the result: a beam can be dated to the year of felling. The underlined sentence supplies the step between them — sliding an undated ring sequence along one from living trees until the patterns line up.

whyWrong.A: No term for a run of narrow rings is defined anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.C: The only limitation mentioned is the survival of the outermost ring, and that appears in the final sentence, not here.
whyWrong.D: "Every tree in a district" is a general statement about how the patterns behave; no particular district is named as an example.

whyCorrect: The first sentence sets up a gap: aeroplane-wing calculations predict too little lift to keep an insect airborne. The underlined sentence supplies the missing physics — a spiral of air clinging to the upper surface, with low pressure inside it pulling the wing up. It introduces the explanation for that shortfall.

whyWrong.A: It does not restate the calculation; it describes a different effect the calculation left out.
whyWrong.B: Far from conceding that the discrepancy is unexplained, it provides the explanation.
whyWrong.C: No experiment or measurement is described — the sentence gives a mechanism.

whyCorrect: Two claims run through the text: the whole basin sings one shared song that changes as alterations pass from singer to singer, and the eastern Australian population dropped its song outright for an arriving western version. The final sentence rules out gradual variation, so the point is that the song is learned and can be swapped whole.

whyWrong.A: The text says every male in a basin sings the same song, not an individual one.
whyWrong.C: No function for the song is proposed anywhere, and feeding territory is never mentioned.
whyWrong.D: Song length is never compared; what travels is the song itself.

whyCorrect: The details all serve one point: a concertina lattice drawn closed by a woven band, roof poles seated by that band's tension, and nothing nailed. Because the frame relies on tension instead of fixed joints, it collapses and travels on two or three animals and goes up in an hour.

whyWrong.A: No seasonal comparison of erection time appears in the text.
whyWrong.B: The crown is described as part of the frame; nothing is said about replacing it.
whyWrong.D: The felt is mentioned as the covering, with no comparison of weights.

whyCorrect: The critic's claim is that the geological attention is avoidance, so the quotation has to show the observing and the postponed conversation in the same breath. Cataloguing cobbles all afternoon "while my mother waited in the kitchen" puts the delay and the person being avoided directly beside the fieldwork.

whyWrong.A: The mismatched roof sheeting is an observation about the farm with no one being avoided in it.
whyWrong.B: Here the conversation actually happens and ends in laughter, so nothing is being put off.
whyWrong.C: The band of ash is pure description; no encounter is deferred or even implied.

whyCorrect: Sæther has to separate low oxygen from poor appetite, which normally arrive together. The chamber study does that: volunteers get low oxygen at sea level while eating a full diet, and they lose muscle at the climbers' rate. With eating held constant, the oxygen shortage is left as the cause.

whyWrong.A: Cold is a third factor and does not distinguish oxygen from appetite; if anything it introduces yet another explanation.
whyWrong.C: Reduced calorie intake supports the rival explanation Sæther is arguing against.
whyWrong.D: Recovery at sea level shows the loss is reversible but says nothing about which of the two causes produced it.
