whyCorrect: Adjustment means the body coping better with the same conditions, so the supporting data must show improvement while the altitude is unchanged. Saturation climbing from 82 to 89 per cent across the five days at a camp that never moved is exactly that.

whyWrong.A: Every reading being below the sea-level 98 per cent shows the climbers were still short of oxygen — it shows the stress, not the adjustment.
whyWrong.B: A breathing rate flat at 23 across three days shows no change and so demonstrates nothing about adjusting.
whyWrong.C: A single day's figure has nothing to compare it with, and it is change over the five days that indicates adjustment.

tips: Evidence of adaptation always needs two points in time; a single reading, however good, cannot show it.

whyCorrect: Steel changes length with temperature, and welded rail has no gaps to absorb that movement — instead the rails are stretched to a set tension as they are fixed down. That tension is only correct for a particular rail temperature, so the laying itself has to happen within a defined temperature range.

whyWrong.A: Ballast packing is a track-support question the passage never raises; the constraint given is thermal.
whyWrong.C: Curvature is not discussed, and welded rail is used on curved lines as well as straight.
whyWrong.D: Whether the work is mechanised has no bearing on the expansion problem the passage sets out.

whyCorrect: Satellite heights are measured from a smooth ellipsoid, but water follows gravity, and the gravity-defined surface departs from that ellipsoid by up to a hundred metres. A canal must fall along the surface water actually settles to, so satellite heights on their own cannot tell the engineer which way the water will run.

whyWrong.A: Age is not the issue; the mismatch is between two different reference surfaces, not between old and new measurements.
whyWrong.B: The passage does not question the precision of satellite positioning — the readings can be precise and still refer to the wrong surface.
whyWrong.D: Season plays no part in the difference between the ellipsoid and the gravity surface.

whyCorrect: "A farmer who lines a leaking ditch and needs less water as a result may find the saved portion forfeit rather than retained" is a complete sentence, and so is "the rule written to stop hoarding now discourages the very efficiency it was meant to encourage." With no conjunction between them, a semicolon is required.

whyWrong.A: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: Unpunctuated, "rather than retained the rule" reads as though the rule were the thing retained.
whyWrong.C: A colon is not followed by and, and what comes next is a second clause rather than an explanation the colon can introduce.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with a When clause that ends at "in a row," and the main clause follows: "no candidate can be said to have beaten every rival." A comma separates an introductory subordinate clause from the main clause.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and the When clause cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete sentence; the opening clause is dependent.
whyWrong.D: With and, both halves fall under When and the sentence never reaches its main clause.

whyCorrect: "The evidence consists of three features found nowhere in an ordinary cave" is a complete sentence, and the gypsum blocks, sulphur crusts and climbing passages are those three features. A colon after a complete clause is the standard way to introduce the list that spells them out.

whyWrong.A: A comma plus and needs an independent clause after it, but the three items are noun phrases with no verb.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation, "an ordinary cave massive blocks of gypsum" runs two noun phrases together with nothing to separate them.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon requires a full clause on each side, and the list is not a clause.

whyCorrect: "The standard advice is to gain no more than three hundred metres ... and to go down at once if the symptoms worsen" is a complete sentence; "acetazolamide, which makes the blood slightly acid and so prompts deeper breathing, is often carried as well" is another. A semicolon joins two independent clauses with no conjunction.

whyWrong.A: Without punctuation the clauses collide and "if the symptoms worsen acetazolamide" reads as though acetazolamide were what worsens.
whyWrong.B: A colon is not followed by a coordinating conjunction, and a full second clause follows rather than an explanation or list.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: "Scanning the recorded data the following morning" has no subject of its own, so the noun that opens the main clause is understood to be doing the scanning. Only a person can scan the data, so the main clause must begin with the duty astronomer.

whyWrong.A: There is a placeholder, so the sentence has nothing that could be doing the scanning — the modifier dangles.
whyWrong.B: This makes the antenna's readings the scanner of the data.
whyWrong.C: Here the wrong readings themselves are scanning the recorded data, which is impossible.

whyCorrect: The possessor is "Every farm," which is singular, and the sentence needs a possessive to attach the bulk tank to it. The singular possessive its is the form that does both.

whyWrong.B: There is an adverb or placeholder and cannot show possession of the bulk tank.
whyWrong.C: It's is the contraction of it is, which produces "must have it is bulk tank tested."
whyWrong.D: Their is plural and does not agree with the singular "Every farm."

commonMistakes: Reading every as plural because it refers to many farms; it always takes singular agreement.

whyCorrect: The commissioning in October is a past event, and the removal of the semaphore arms happened before it — the sentence says "already." An action completed before a past reference point takes the past perfect.

whyWrong.B: Will have sets up a future deadline, but October has already passed in this narrative.
whyWrong.C: Is cannot combine with been taken down to place the removal before the October date, and it puts the sentence in the present.
whyWrong.D: Has gives the present perfect, which ties the removal to now rather than to the earlier October commissioning.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences say a tuned mass can be set against a building's single sway period. The third says the same device does much less in an earthquake, because the shaking arrives across many periods. A limitation set against the capability just described calls for a contrastive transition.

whyWrong.A: In short announces a summary, but the third sentence adds a new and opposing case.
whyWrong.B: Therefore would make the earthquake shortcoming a consequence of the damper working well in wind, which is not the relationship.
whyWrong.D: Likewise claims the earthquake case runs parallel to the wind case, when the point is that it does not.

whyCorrect: The first sentence lists reasonable requirements a voting rule ought to meet. The second reports Arrow's proof that no rule can meet them all when three or more options are ranked. The result runs against what the first sentence leads you to expect, so the transition is concessive.

whyWrong.A: Similarly presents the second sentence as another instance of the first, but it contradicts the hope the first sets up.
whyWrong.B: In short promises a condensed restatement, and the proof is new information, not a summary.
whyWrong.D: For instance would make Arrow's theorem an example of the desirable conditions rather than a demonstration that they conflict.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says heating kills both the harmful bacteria and the mixed population that would have ripened the cheese on its own. The second states what follows: with the native flora gone, the cheese depends wholly on added cultures and its flavour is narrower and more predictable. That is a consequence.

whyWrong.A: By contrast sets two things against each other, but the second sentence follows directly from the first.
whyWrong.B: For example would make the pasteurised cheese an instance of heating milk, whereas it is the outcome of it.
whyWrong.C: Nevertheless marks a result that runs against expectation, and this result is exactly what killing the native flora would produce.

whyCorrect: Explaining why the villages pooled milk requires the constraint and the response together: no single household produced enough in a day for the big wheels that keep and travel best, so the day's milk was combined and each household credited with its share.

whyWrong.B: The written record and the elected auditors describe how the scheme was administered, not why it existed.
whyWrong.C: The advantage of large wheels is half the reason, but with no mention of the shortfall it does not explain pooling.
whyWrong.D: This states that pooling happened and when, without giving any cause.

whyCorrect: The goal is why timing is centralised rather than left to individual subaks, so the sentence has to name benefits that only coordination can produce. Two notes give them: flooding a whole block at once drowns its pests, and staggering the blocks keeps peak demand inside the stream's supply. Both depend on subaks acting in concert.

whyWrong.B: The tunnels and channels describe the irrigation system, not why scheduling is done collectively.
whyWrong.C: Defining a subak identifies who the actors are without saying why they cannot each set their own dates.
whyWrong.D: This states that the temples set the dates — the fact to be explained, not the explanation.

whyCorrect: A funding case needs a comparable number, and the software's contribution is that it converts canopy effects — rainfall intercepted, pollutants removed, cooling energy saved — into money. The survey result, a return of about $26 a year for every dollar of maintenance, is the figure a department can take to a budget meeting.

whyWrong.A: The inputs describe how the model is fed and produce no argument for money.
whyWrong.C: The competition with roads and drains sets up the problem but does not show how the software helps solve it.
whyWrong.D: Saying the software measures what a canopy does stops short of the pricing and the result that make the case.

whyCorrect: The passage describes a strict priority rule: in a dry year the oldest right takes its whole allotment before a later one gets anything, and rights are not reduced proportionally. Seniority therefore determines who actually receives water, and the sentence contrasts the blank with "ceremonial" — a mere honour.

whyWrong.A: Recent describes when a right was acquired and does not contrast with ceremonial at all; the seniority that matters here is old, not recent.
whyWrong.C: Symbolic is a near-synonym of ceremonial, so the sentence would contradict itself.
whyWrong.D: Negotiable would mean the order could be bargained over, but the passage describes it as applied automatically.

whyCorrect: Quarter-sawing wastes wood and takes longer — that is the yield given up — and what it buys is stated directly: the finished boards "move very little afterwards," unlike flat-sawn boards that cup as they dry. The blank names that resistance to movement.

whyWrong.A: The passage says nothing about the appearance or figure of the boards.
whyWrong.B: Novelty is irrelevant to a long-established sawing method chosen for how the wood behaves.
whyWrong.C: Quantity is what the method sacrifices, not what it gains — it is another word for yield.

whyCorrect: The clause after the blank explains the reaction: the prose withholds exactly the commentary these readers expect. A dying man remarking on weapon fashions with nobody calling the moment terrible unsettles a reader trained on later narrative, so the blank needs a word for that unsettled feeling.

whyWrong.B: Sentimental describes the emotional commentary the sagas conspicuously refuse to supply.
whyWrong.C: Ornate contradicts a level voice that reports killings without embellishment.
whyWrong.D: Reassuring is the opposite of what the withheld commentary produces in a reader expecting it.

whyCorrect: The passage describes a rule with no exceptions: the section counts as occupied the instant a train enters, and no second train may be admitted until word comes back, with no driver left to judge distances. The blank must name that absoluteness, set against leaving the decision to the crew.

whyWrong.A: Occasional would mean the rule applies only sometimes, but it governs every entry into the block.
whyWrong.B: Informal contradicts a system built on a fixed signalling procedure between boxes.
whyWrong.D: Advisory is close to the alternative the sentence rejects — a rule the men on the footplate could weigh up rather than obey.

whyCorrect: The stalks make no lift; what they do is resist a turn so that sensors at their base can read the strain. That is a device for measuring the fly's rotation, so the blank needs a word for a sensing device — set against the idea that the stalks are just reduced wings.

whyWrong.A: Afterthought suggests something added without purpose, but the structure has a clear and active function.
whyWrong.B: Ornament implies no function at all, which the strain sensors contradict.
whyWrong.D: Obstacle would make the stalks a hindrance to flight, whereas they supply information that guides it.

whyCorrect: The final sentence hangs on an absence: seismographs on the far side record only the compressional arrival. That absence means something only if you know a shearing wave cannot cross a liquid, which is precisely what the underlined sentence supplies. It provides the physics that converts a missing signal into evidence of a molten core.

whyWrong.A: The reliability of the instruments is never questioned; their records are treated as sound.
whyWrong.B: The two wave types are already described in the first sentence; the underlined sentence adds a property of one of them.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text disputes it — the closing sentence builds on it.

whyCorrect: Follow the three moves. The text first identifies a single manuscript as the source of nearly all this poetry; then it states what cannot be established — how much older the poems are, and that most have no second copy; then it points to the eight missing leaves that removed part of a heroic cycle.

whyWrong.A: No move from oral performance to print is traced; the text stays with one manuscript.
whyWrong.B: The text says the poems are older than the book by an unknown margin, which is the opposite of arguing for a later composition.
whyWrong.D: Only one manuscript is discussed, so no comparison or preference between two is possible.

whyCorrect: The text gives the reason in the same sentence as the paradox: enlarging the chamber cost Alabama a seat "because the fractions did not all grow at the same rate." Under a rule that hands out leftover seats by ranking fractions, uneven growth in those fractions can push a state down the ranking even though the total number of seats went up.

whyWrong.A: No change in population is mentioned — the anomaly arises from the arithmetic of a fixed set of populations at two chamber sizes.
whyWrong.C: The rule described gives leftover seats to the states with the largest fractions, not to the smallest states.
whyWrong.D: Indivisibility is the general reason fractions exist at all; it does not explain why one particular state lost a seat when the house grew.

whyCorrect: The text pairs a benefit with a cost. Taking a few trees from every size class every ten or fifteen years leaves the stand permanently covered and mixed in age; the price is small yields per entry, permanently maintained roads, and a higher cost per cubic metre than clear-felling a block.

whyWrong.B: No comparison of timber volume per hectare is made — the comparison is about cost per cubic metre.
whyWrong.C: The passage says the canopy closes over the gaps within a few seasons, not decades.
whyWrong.D: It says the opposite: the roads have to be kept open permanently.

whyCorrect: The stated explanation is that bitter peptides are only broken down further once the paste has stopped being acid. Supporting data must therefore link falling acidity to falling bitterness: as pH climbs 5.2, 5.6, 6.0, 6.3, the number of bitter wheels drops 9, 5, 2, 0 at each step.

whyWrong.A: The week 2 figure alone shows bitterness was common early but does not connect it to the acidity of the paste.
whyWrong.C: Moisture also falls across the study, but the explanation in the text is about acidity, not water content, so this pairs the wrong variable.
whyWrong.D: The final pH is one endpoint with no bitterness figure attached and no trend.

tips: Read the stated mechanism first, then find the two columns it names — data about a third variable cannot support it however neatly it trends.

whyCorrect: The claim is that the silence is a strategy, so the quotation must show Hrafn choosing to wait for a reason. Counting the winters like coin and judging that a case at the Thing is worth more than a body in a ditch gives both the deliberation and the calculation behind it.

whyWrong.A: His wife's taunt reports how others read the silence, not what Hrafn intended by it.
whyWrong.B: This shows the silence and the contempt it drew — the impression of weakness the scholar's claim argues against.
whyWrong.D: The hard winter and the sheep are narrative background with no bearing on Hrafn's intentions.

whyCorrect: The second suggestion ties the falling pitch to a rising population — more whales within earshot means a quieter, less far-carrying call suffices. The table supports it only if the two move together, and they do: frequency drops 22.0, 20.5, 19.0, 17.5 while the estimate climbs 1,200, 1,600, 2,300, 3,400.

whyWrong.B: The tripling of the population is half the relationship; with no mention of the call frequency it cannot support a claim about why the pitch fell.
whyWrong.C: A single frequency reading has nothing to compare it with and no population figure attached.
whyWrong.D: One decade's drop in frequency omits the population column entirely, which is the variable the second suggestion depends on.

whyCorrect: When the water takes up the load, the grain contacts are relieved and the ground behaves like a heavy liquid. A liquid cannot support a foundation, so the building settles into it or leans — the structure itself is not being torn apart, the ground under it has stopped holding it up.

whyWrong.A: Vibration damage to the structure is a different failure mode; the passage is about the ground losing strength, not about the building being shaken to pieces.
whyWrong.C: No slope or fault is described, and the mechanism given works on level ground.
whyWrong.D: Fire is a real earthquake hazard but has nothing to do with the loss of grain contact the passage explains.

whyCorrect: The key fact is that the same ability arose by different genetic routes in Europe, Arabia and East Africa. Independent appearances in separate herding populations point to an advantage strong enough to be selected for again and again wherever milk was available.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text restricts the advantage to famine; the repeated appearance suggests a persistent benefit, not an occasional one.
whyWrong.C: The passage gives no comparison of the strength of the benefit between regions.
whyWrong.D: Cereal growing is never mentioned; the common factor named is herding.

whyCorrect: "The legends on those coins run in Greek script and the deities on their reverses are Iranian, Greek and Indian by turns" is a complete sentence, and "the coinage is one of the few sources showing how the dynasty presented itself" is another. With no conjunction between them, a semicolon is needed.

whyWrong.A: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation, "by turns the coinage" runs the two clauses together with no boundary.
whyWrong.C: A colon is never followed by and, and a second full clause follows rather than an explanation or list.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with a Because clause ending at "diverted," and the main clause is "signalling engineers describe the arrangement as failing safe." An introductory subordinate clause is set off with a comma.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and the Because clause cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete sentence; what precedes it here is a dependent clause.
whyWrong.D: With and, the sentence keeps both halves inside the Because clause and never supplies a main clause.

commonMistakes: Misreading signalling as a verb after the blank; here it modifies engineers, so the main clause begins with the subject.

whyCorrect: "Although the observatory at Green Bank sits inside a zone in which transmitters are restricted by law" is a subordinate clause, and the main clause follows: "its engineers still drive the local roads with a receiver." A comma separates the two.

whyWrong.A: With and, both halves fall under Although, so the sentence has no main clause and is a fragment.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and the Although clause is dependent.
whyWrong.D: A colon must be preceded by a complete sentence, which the Although clause is not.

whyCorrect: "The insect is far denser than the liquid it stands on" and "it never breaks through unless the surface has been fouled with detergent" are both complete sentences. Joined by the coordinating conjunction and, they need a comma before that conjunction.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon already links two independent clauses by itself; putting and after it is redundant and non-standard.
whyWrong.C: A colon introduces an explanation or a list and is never followed by a coordinating conjunction.
whyWrong.D: Without the comma the two clauses run together, and "the liquid it stands on and it never breaks through" reads as a single tangled string.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The board's collection," which is singular. The phrase "together with several boxwood scales" is set off by commas and does not add to the subject, so the verb stays singular.

whyWrong.A: Are is plural and agrees with "scales" or "sight rules" rather than with collection.
whyWrong.B: Have been is likewise plural, so it fails to match the singular subject.
whyWrong.C: Were is plural; the number, not the tense, is what rules it out.

commonMistakes: Counting a together with phrase as part of the subject — only and makes a subject plural.

whyCorrect: The relative pronoun that refers back to "the few sites in the region," not to "one" — the surveying is what those few sites have in common. With a plural antecedent, the auxiliary is plural.

whyWrong.A: Is is singular and cannot combine with been surveyed to give the present perfect the sentence needs.
whyWrong.B: Has agrees with one, but the clause describes the whole group of sites that share this record.
whyWrong.D: Having is a participle, leaving the relative clause without a finite verb.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The number," which is singular, and "of young limes lost to drought last year" is a prepositional phrase. "Last year" puts the statement in the past, so the singular past-tense verb is right.

whyWrong.A: Have been is plural and agrees with "limes" instead of "number."
whyWrong.C: Are is both plural and present, clashing with the singular subject and with "last year."
whyWrong.D: Were is plural; the number takes a singular verb even though a number of takes a plural one.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the benefit of living at altitude — more oxygen-carrying capacity.
